title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–7)
hook: the second telling: God shapes a human from the dust and breathes into its nose

segments.voice: Yesterday, imago Dei: every human made in God's image, and your line was very good.

Turn one page in Genesis and the story starts again. Chapter one told it from high above: days, lights, a world spoken into order, people made last. Chapter two drops down to the ground. No rain yet, no one to work the soil, just a mist coming up from the earth and watering it. And instead of speaking from a distance, God gets close. Hands in the dirt. The first chapter was a cathedral. The second is a workshop.
screen: `THE STORY STARTS AGAIN.` → `FROM HIGH ABOVE, THEN THE GROUND.` → `HANDS IN THE DIRT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Formed: the Hebrew verb is the one used for a potter shaping clay. Then a pun English loses. The ground is adamah. The human made from it is adam. Earthling from the earth. Adam isn't first a name here; it's a word for a human being, a creature of soil. Then the breath. God doesn't speak this one into being. God leans in and breathes into its nose, and the clay becomes a living soul, in Hebrew a nefesh, a living being. This telling differs from chapter one. The order changes, and even the name for God changes: chapter one says God, chapter two says the LORD God, the personal name. Many scholars think two older accounts were set side by side. Many Christians read them as two views of one event, a wide shot and a close-up. Either way, the book kept both. And the close-up says something about a person. You are dust, made of the same stuff as the ground under your shoes. And you are breath, given by God from close up. Not one or the other. In churches that keep Ash Wednesday, the ashes often go on with words from the next chapter: dust thou art. And many Christians link the breath with the Spirit; in both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit can also mean breath.
screen: `FORMED, LIKE A POTTER WITH CLAY.` · `ADAM FROM ADAMAH: EARTHLING.` · `GOD BREATHES INTO ITS NOSE.` · `TWO TELLINGS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `AND MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Feel your weight, your feet on the floor, your body heavy in the chair: that's the dust. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, five times, slower each time, and notice the air coming in: that's the breath. If you pray, you can give thanks for the breath you didn't have to make.
Adamah. The Hebrew word for ground, the soil a human, adam, was shaped from, then given breath to live.
Your line: dust with breath in it. Both halves, every day. Day three hundred thirty-five.

screen: `DAY 335 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GARDEN AND THE NAMES.`

chat.meaning: Chapter two starts again on the ground, with a new name for God. Scholars see two older accounts; many Christians see two views of one event.

adam.meaning: Hebrew for a human being, a creature of the soil

nefesh.meaning: Hebrew for a living being, what the clay becomes

notes: Audit (y2 second sample): the teach said Christians remember the dust 'every Ash Wednesday', which overstates it (not every church keeps Ash Wednesday) and claimed they remember the breath 'every time they talk about the Spirit'; both lines rewritten. Note Genesis 2:7 uses neshamah, not ruach, for breath; the new line speaks only of the general breath/spirit overlap (ruach, pneuma). Confirm.
Two readings of the two creation accounts (scholarly view of two older sources; many Christians' 'wide shot and close-up') given without ranking; confirm fair.
Hebrew yatsar ('formed') is used of potters (e.g. Jeremiah 18); confirm.
nefesh chayyah glossed 'a living being'; confirm.
Ash Wednesday wording: several formulas are used ('Remember that you are dust...' or 'Repent and believe the Gospel'); script says 'many ministers repeat words from the next chapter'. Confirm.
